stories.headline: OpenAI's model claims matrix multiplication's exponent is exactly 9/4, killing the ω = 2 dream
stories.why_read: If it holds, one of computer science's oldest open questions is settled, by a model, and the answer is that matrix multiply can never get close to quadratic.
body: A 111-page preprint dated November 24 in OpenAI's math repository, which collects manuscripts "produced by an unnamed internal OpenAI model," claims that the exponent of square matrix multiplication is 9/4 over every field. The 9/4 upper bound was already known; the new result is the matching lower bound: any formal arithmetic circuit multiplying two n × n matrices needs at least n^(9/4)/2 multiplication or division gates. The proof argues that a smaller exponent would compress tensor networks enough to violate a lower bound for testing whether entries in several independent lists are distinct.

That would refute the long-standing conjecture that ω = 2. OpenAI's README cautions that not every result in the repo has a Lean formalization, that unformalized results "could have issues," and that the manuscripts are best read as "raw research data, rather than polished academic papers." On HN, where it drew 700+ points, commenters stressed the point is a tight Θ(n^2.25), not just another upper bound, and asked whether the upper-bound techniques could ever become practical GPU kernels.

stories.headline: Tesla registers 49 more Cybercabs in Texas, and its autonomous fleet passes Waymo's
stories.why_read: Cybercabs are now more than half of Tesla's 1,556-vehicle Texas autonomy fleet, the clearest sign yet the purpose-built car is scaling.
body: Late on November 24, Tesla added 49 new 2027 Cybercabs to the Texas DMV list, according to trackers who confirmed the additions by VIN and X's news summary. That brings Tesla's autonomous vehicles registered in Texas to 1,556: 822 Cybercabs and 734 Model Ys, the first time the fleet has topped 1,500.
Per the same summary, that puts Tesla 151 vehicles ahead of Waymo's 1,405 on the list, with the steering-wheel-free Cybercab now the majority of the fleet as Tesla runs service in Austin and Dallas.

stories.headline: OpenAI says GPT-6 can design proteins with reasoning and code alone, and some of them bind in the lab
stories.why_read: A general model matching specialized protein tools on many tasks is a big step toward "describe the molecule you want" biology.
body: In a new preprint, OpenAI says its GPT-6 family can design new protein structures and sequences using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools, without calling specialized biology models. An internal research model matched or beat specialized models on most computational tasks, though predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

Lab tests with partner Onava (where specialized models still helped supply sequences and pick candidates) showed binding for all five chosen targets: 35 of 322 minibinders (10.9%) hit their intended target. Asked to redesign the binding loops of six small antibodies against IL-4Rα, 128 of 182 designs (70%) still bound. OpenAI notes the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Neon breaks Google's Day-1 usage record, and Perplexity's volume doubles in three days
stories.why_read: The model people in Anand's feed are switching to: Perplexity passed 120B Neon tokens and Cursor users say they now daily-drive it.
body: Per X's news summary, Sundar Pichai said Gemini 4 Neon set a Day-1 usage record on Google's paid APIs, with daily tokens up 82 percent in six weeks; developers are praising its coding and reasoning and its 1-million-token context window. Aravind Srinivas said Perplexity has passed 120B tokens of Neon usage, doubling daily volume in three days, with 36B on Monday alone.

Srinivas puts it "somewhere between Opus and Fable in intelligence level, but with a far better response style and usability," and says Perplexity will tune its harness around Neon's formatting and task duration. Lauren Tan (@poteto): "never thought i'd say this but i am now daily driving gemini neon in cursor."

stories.headline: Claude artifacts can now be installed as desktop apps on Mac and Windows
stories.why_read: Small personal tools Claude builds can now live in the Dock with your connectors, notifications and a menu bar item.
body: Anthropic's ClaudeDevs account announced that you can ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app," and open it like any other app on Mac or Windows. Installed apps can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item.

Paweł Huryn notes the trade-off: artifacts use your Claude account, so there's no separate login, database or API key, but only you and your team can save data. For apps other agents publish or that call other APIs directly he'd use Cloudflare, and for customers, build your own app.

stories.headline: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 packs a Qwen3.8 27B agent into 5.9 GB
stories.why_read: Open weights under Apache 2.0, strong agentic tool use, and about 200 tokens/s on an RTX 4090: local coding agents keep getting more real.
body: PrismML's Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, based on Qwen3.8 27B, keeps its predecessor's 5.9 GB footprint while substantially improving agentic coding, multi-turn tool use and multi-step task execution. PrismML says it completes tasks in fewer turns and tokens than Bonsai 2 and narrows the gap to the full-precision base model.

On a single H100 it generates 291 tokens/s with multi-token prediction and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s; on an RTX 4090 it does 204 tokens/s. It runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Macs, iPhones and iPads via MLX, with weights under Apache 2.0.

stories.headline: Lucid, Nuro and Uber pull the safety drivers in the Bay Area
stories.why_read: Uber's 35,000-vehicle bet just went fully driverless on public roads, which observers say beats Tesla to that milestone in California.
body: Lucid, Nuro and Uber began fully driverless robotaxi testing on public roads in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos and Sunnyvale on November 24, after nearly a year of supervised runs, per X's news summary. The vehicles are Lucid Gravity SUVs running Nuro's autonomy stack, owned and operated by Uber for its app. "Nobody in the front seat," Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi posted.

Employee rides start soon and public service is planned for early 2027. Uber has committed to buying at least 35,000 of the vehicles. Observers noted Lucid beat Tesla to driverless testing in California, while Tesla's Austin service undercuts on price: $3.01 a mile for Cybercab versus $3.45 for UberX, per the summary.

stories.headline: GreyNoise uncovers a campaign that compromised Check Point management servers at 22 organizations
stories.why_read: If you run Check Point, check your Security Management Servers now; the actor likely used LLM agents for the whole kill chain.
body: GreyNoise says it caught an intrusion campaign, tracked as GT13, against Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed activity between October 17 and November 2, 2026, hitting at least 22 organizations across finance, energy, government, transportation, mining and manufacturing in Europe, Asia, Australia and the U.S. The actor used 99 IP addresses and a compromised relay box to store results and data stolen from 24 servers.

CVEs used or attempted include a Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script (CVE-2026-16232), Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti and Windows NetLogon bugs. One entry point: reconstructing V8's Math.random() state from HFS login cookies to forge an admin session. GreyNoise doesn't attribute it to a known group but believes the actor used LLMs and agentic systems for scanning, exploitation and tooling.

stories.headline: Sandboxed models can still talk to each other through a shared inference server
stories.why_read: A concrete, reproducible side channel through vLLM's kernel choices, with direct implications for anyone running agent monitors on shared infrastructure.
body: Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa show two agents on the same vLLM server can communicate without messages or a shared filesystem, by influencing how the engine sizes steps and chooses kernels. In a color-guessing game Bob identified Alice's color in 1,221 of 1,221 rounds; in an untrusted-monitoring setup, a colluding monitor let through 354 of 354 signaled "attacks" while still catching 85 to 92% of honeypots.

The authors admit the setups are contrived (models were told the protocol and fine-tuned), but say frontier models can learn similar protocols in context with scaffolding. The suggested check: run models in different server configurations and confirm outputs are bit-identical.

stories.headline: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B looped transformer that runs on a 32GB Mac
stories.why_read: A new strong open-weights coder under 100B parameters from Mira Murati's lab, plus a fresh NVIDIA Vera server in the office.
body: Per X's news summary, Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4-billion-parameter looped transformer aimed at agentic coding and reasoning that runs locally on 32GB Macs or similar machines, with up to a 1M-token context and vision support.

Per the summary, it scores 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified, topping open-weights models under 100B parameters. Unsloth already has a fine-tuning notebook, and Murati posted photos of NVIDIA delivering a Vera CPU server to the office.

stories.headline: DeepMind's Gemini 4 agent teams find quantum algorithms up to 290x cheaper
stories.why_read: AI agents doing verified algorithm research, with fusion and chemistry simulation among the beneficiaries.
body: Per X's news summary, Google DeepMind ran parallel teams of Gemini 4 agents, debating on shared wikis, to discover more efficient quantum algorithms. One key subroutine cut estimated resource costs by 290 times.

Gains also reached fusion energy simulation (11.8x cheaper), photochemistry (8x) and drug modeling (2.5x, with fewer qubits), all verified mathematically with the Lean theorem prover. The library is open source on GitHub.

stories.headline: Anthropic's seven co-founders sold about $2 billion of stock at the IPO price
stories.why_read: The founders cashed out identically at $83, and the stock has since dipped below that.
body: Per X's news summary, each of Anthropic's seven co-founders, including Dario and Daniela Amodei, sold 3,378,378 Class A shares at the $83 IPO price, nearly $2 billion in total that went to them rather than the company. The sales were disclosed in the prospectus; the Amodeis each still hold stakes worth around $20 billion.

The stock debuted at $111.50 on November 19 but closed at $81.90 on November 24, below the IPO price, amid tech-sector pressure. Commenters contrasted it with SpaceX's June IPO, where Musk sold nothing.

stories.headline: XPENG shows driverless robotaxi rides and seven IRON humanoids at AI Day
stories.why_read: China's EV makers are converging on Tesla's playbook: Robotaxi plus humanoids on custom chips.
body: At AI Day 2026 in Guangzhou, XPENG gave international testers fully driverless Robotaxi rides with no safety driver, powered by its Turing AI chips, per X's news summary. It plans a global rollout next year and a YOYO-01 model in 2027.
It also showed seven IRON humanoid robots, 170 cm tall with 76 degrees of freedom and 2,250 TOPS of compute, that walked and talked with the crowd. Mass production of IRON starts in January 2027.

stories.headline: Claude Code's /ship hands off the boring work after you open a PR
stories.why_read: CI failures, review comments and merge conflicts become an agent's job, and you don't need admin rights to try it.
body: Anthropic's guide to Claude Ship lays out three agents for post-PR work: Code Review (generally available), PR Steward and Claude Approvals (both beta). You run /ship in your own Claude Code session to open a PR, review it, and keep working on what comes back; /steward looks after a PR you already opened; /code-review finds bugs before anyone else looks.

The post targets developers and tech leads on GitHub without admin privileges. You save what you learn to files in the repo for the team to review, and admins only get involved if the team wants agents doing this automatically on everyone's PRs.

stories.headline: Uber went from one agent skill to 5,000 in a year
stories.why_read: Real numbers on enterprise skills: 1 million invocations a month, and removing one skill meant 6x more tool errors.
body: Praveen Neppalli says Uber had exactly one agent skill a year ago and now has more than 5,000, built by thousands of employees and invoked over a million times a month. Uber's marketplace is model- and agent-agnostic, working across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and internal agents.

His lessons: as models improve, the best fix for a skill is sometimes deleting parts of it; skills change the economics (in one experiment, removing a skill caused 6x more tool errors and 31% longer runs); and Uber's agents file bug reports themselves when they hit broken workflows.

stories.headline: How to build a software factory your team will actually use
stories.why_read: A follow-up to yesterday's factory-engineering frame, this time with YAML blueprints, human gates and merge-risk scoring.
body: Ben Holmes defines a software factory as "an automation loop in the cloud that orchestrates agents to build better and better software over time," and warns that teams who only automate the loop end up with a black box or a "slop cannon" producing PRs no one reads.

His deep dive turns a markdown skill into a YAML blueprint (in the format Warp Factories uses), with typed inputs and outputs per stage and separate worker sandboxes. It adds triage and spec stages where humans judge requirements, gives agents a computer to verify their own work, and scores merge risk so reviewers know which PRs need the closest look.

stories.headline: Safari now ships with an MCP server for agents
stories.why_read: Turn on one setting and Claude can drive Safari to test and tune your site.
body: NatashaTheRobot points out that Safari now comes with an MCP server: enable "remote automation and external agents" and an agent like Claude can work against Safari directly, for example to optimize your website for it.
For anyone who has fought WebKit-only bugs, an official agent hook into the browser is a small but welcome change.

stories.headline: Ask the AI to find your implicit state machines, model them in TLA+, and find bugs
stories.why_read: Tobi Lütke's tip turned into a skill found 10+ bugs. Formal methods just got a lot cheaper.
body: Anton Zolotov heard Shopify's Tobi Lütke suggest asking AI to identify implicit state machines in a codebase, map their states and transitions, and build a TLA+ model to find bugs. He had an AI grab the podcast episode and turn the advice into a skill, and says it found more than 10 bugs.
It pairs with Ian Duncan's essay on HN arguing that LLMs remove the time pressure that used to stop careful engineers from writing the TLA+ model or the property test they knew they should.

stories.headline: exe.dev: Big Serverless has taken us for fools
stories.why_read: A spicy case for "dev is prod" on one small VM when agents write the code faster than you can build pipelines.
body: exe.dev argues that if you develop software agentically, deploying can take longer than writing it, so building pipelines before you have users is premature optimization. Instead of splitting low-traffic software into serverless functions to save pennies, use a small VM, "pay thirty times as much ($1 per day!)," and focus on whether the software makes sense.
The proof is the blog itself: it runs on a single VM, with a bespoke CMS on the same VM, edited by a coding agent on that same VM. exe.dev notes that's not how it builds its own backend services.

stories.headline: Ask HN: Anthropic accuses a company of distilling. How do you prove you aren't?
stories.why_read: A cautionary tale for anyone running automated evals against a frontier API.
body: An HN user says Anthropic accused their company of using its API for distillation and gave them 24 hours to prove otherwise. They say they don't train their own models; the only usage they think could be flagged is automated regression benchmarks run whenever they change AI settings.
Their question, which drew 250+ comments: how do you prove a negative like this without breaking your users' privacy?

stories.headline: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
stories.why_read: Dangling DNS records pointing at released AWS Elastic IPs are still exploitable in 2026. Go audit your A records.
body: Intruder researchers repeatedly allocated and released AWS Elastic IPs, checking each against A records pulled from public bug bounty scopes, until they landed addresses that dangling DNS still pointed to. Among the hits were real US Treasury subdomains, reported and fixed through a bug bounty program.
Cost: about $3 per valid takeover, after AWS auto-approved a quota bump to 25 Elastic IPs per region. They covered under 1% of the IP space, so many more are likely out there for attackers.

stories.headline: Serving Qwen across 5,600 AWS Lambdas, at 80x the cost
stories.why_read: A fun, honest experiment that shows exactly why inference wants a GPU.
body: The author split a 9.3 GB Qwen3.5-4B fine-tune into its 32 layers of about 225 MB each, so each fits in a 3 GB Lambda, and ran one job per layer per block of tokens, passing state through S3 in a 32-layer staircase.

It worked, but reading a 4,000-token document took 17 seconds and cost 3.4 cents, or $8.40 per million tokens, more than 80 times Google's hosted Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10. His takeaway: model engineering is easy now, and you need a GPU.

stories.headline: Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS cap by letting the compositor do the work
stories.why_read: A clever hack that makes web UIs feel native on 120 Hz iPhones without flipping hidden flags.
body: Unless you enable a buried developer flag, WebKit on iOS limits requestAnimationFrame and touch events to 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen. The author's trick is to route interactions through a scrollable area, because scrolling runs on the compositor thread with no JavaScript round-trip.

Reading scroll position outside the renderer lets you treat a scroll region like a trackpad, an infinitely scrolling trackball with native momentum, or a source of native bounce, and apply that physics to your animations.

stories.headline: A faster way to extract hexadecimal digits of π without the ones before
stories.why_read: Thirty years after BBP, a rearranged Euler series cuts the work by about 40%.
body: Robert Smith presents a new digit-extraction algorithm for π that beats term-by-term BBP, Bellard and Huvent formulas on operation count. Against Huvent's eight-term formula it uses about 61% fewer divisions and 38% fewer full modular exponentiations.

The trick is grouping terms by a common odd denominator so four remainders can be added and divided once, and reaching related powers of two by multiplication. He says that saves about a million full exponentiations per million hex places and runs in nearly 40% less wall-clock time.

stories.headline: PenGPT: tiny transformers that write in your hand and sketch from text
stories.why_read: A lovely Bitter Lesson case study: 80% data, 15% speed, 5% architecture.
body: Sam Greydanus built two small transformers: a 6M-parameter model that writes print and cursive and picks up a new writer's hand from a few words, and a 54M-parameter model that draws from a text prompt. The handwriting data came from scans traced back into strokes, 495,590 words by 1,255 writers; drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets.

His ablations show data and augmentation matter most: without augmentation, the drawing model stops following prompts almost entirely. He flags that Claude wrote the post's text and says he'll rewrite it himself over Thanksgiving.

stories.headline: A rewritable display that holds an image for months with no power
stories.why_read: Phase-change materials could make near-zero-power signs and screens. Real chemistry with an energy payoff.
body: Researchers at Australia's TMOS centre, from RMIT and ANU, report in Advanced Photonics Research the first reflective display based on antimony selenide (Sb2Se3) that can hold an image for months without power, while being reliably reusable and offering a wide colour gamut.

Antimony selenide is a phase-change material: heat, light or electricity switch it between amorphous and crystalline states, and once switched it stays put without continuous power. "This is a new way to create energy-efficient displays," says lead researcher Dr Phuong Yen Le.

stories.headline: Old Nvidia and ATI tech demos, running again in your browser
stories.why_read: Pure nostalgia for anyone who remembers when a new GPU shipped with a showpiece demo.
body: A Show HN gallery rebuilds the demos graphics cards shipped with, from the original files, and runs them in the browser: from Borg, a cube with nine textures in five passes as the first card with two texture units drew it, to Ruby's first mission and Paul Debevec's high-dynamic-range glass and gold balls.
There's fur, caustics, Animusic's self-playing machine, and smoke and water simulated on the card itself that you can stir with the pointer.

stories.headline: A map of the 17-million-line Lean Riemann proof looks like a nervous system
stories.why_read: A striking picture of what AI-scale formal mathematics actually looks like.
body: Mirza posted a visualization of the 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, 175,000 files of machine-checked code, and says the resulting map looks like a biological nervous system. "We just entered the era of alien mathematics," he wrote.
It's the AI-assisted attempt covered here Monday, and with today's matrix-multiplication claim, the week's theme is clear: models are producing math at a scale humans can only map, not read.

stories.headline: Steve Yegge: Software Factories, Escape from Trash Mountain
stories.why_read: "Writing code got cheap. Cleaning up the pile didn't." A talk on keeping agents useful as context runs away.
body: AI.Engineer posted Steve Yegge's full Code Summit talk, "Software Factories: Escape from Trash Mountain," on software factories, runaway context and the work of keeping agents useful.
Its framing is that writing code got cheap but cleaning up the pile didn't, a counterweight to the week's factory-building enthusiasm.

stories.headline: A once anti-EV dad talked to Grok for 7.5 hours on a Model Y road trip
stories.why_read: A sweet, funny glimpse of in-car AI winning over skeptics, until the credits ran out.
body: Per X's news summary, one woman's parents called from the road after 7.5 hours of nonstop Grok chatter in their new Model Y, asking how to get more credits. Her dad, once anti-EV, used voice commands to toggle the AC, and her stepmom requested a 30-minute story.
Musk shared that Grok makes road trips fun. Other owners say they chat with it on commutes instead of the radio, though some note mic issues.
